# Introduction

## Outline

* P1: Immunomodulatory receptors are key therapeutic targets but generate limiting off-target effects.
    + Molecules that interact with surface receptors are the largest class of therapeutics.
    + Immunomodulatory receptors often dictate immune cell function and are thus involved in a broad range of immune-mediated diseases.
    + Two properties of immune receptors:
        * Shared receptor expression across cells of different functions leads to off-target binding
        * Cellular pleiotropy leads to counteractive signals in off-target cells
    + Combined, these features lead to off-target binding which produces signals that counteract the desired effect (at best) and generate severe adverse effects (at worst)
    + Immunomodulatory ligands are rarely adopted because of severe adverse effects that arise from off-target binding.
* P2: Protein engineering efforts have reduced off-target binding through avidity-dependent targeting.
    + The promise of immunomodulatory molecules has spurred extensive protein engineering efforts aimed at reducing off-target binding
    + Chief among these are multivalent, affinity-engineered cytokine muteins fused to targeted antibody scaffolds (targeted, multispecific cytokine fusions) 
    + Coordinated changes in affinity and valency allow these molecules to preferentially bind target cells despite modest differences in receptor expression between target and off-target populations.
    + These molecules owe this so-called cell-type selectivity to avidity effects wherein low-affinity, multivalent molecules require high receptor density to bind effectively
* P3: Often, binding is all that matters.
    + Multispecific molecules with decoupled signaling and targeting domains have been shown to further enhance cell-type selectivity
    + In these cases, high-affinity and/or high-valency targeting subunits direct signal domain binding toward target cells, while low-affinity signal domains are unable to bind off-target cells despite high signal receptor density
    + Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates use targeting domains to direct cytotoxic payloads based on surface protein expression
    + Considering only the targeting function of surface proteins reveals a vast number of potential surface targets which might be exploited alone or in combination.
* P4: Combinatorial complexity has left the development of multispecific, targeted therapeutics unguided.
    + Evolution has granted us with thousands of unique surface proteins
    + These proteins may, in some combination, facilitate perfectly selective delivery of signal to any given cell type
    + However, the number of possible combinations of surface proteins is combinatorially large
    + This complexity has left the field of multispecificity unguided and siloed.
    + Even systematic explorations neglect to comprehensively evaluate the selectivity of the large space of possible targets, especially across different target cell types
* P5: Here, we use a high-throughput computational platform to systematically explore the multi-receptor targeting space and identify key properties of multispecificity.

## Body

Immunomodulatory receptors are key therapeutic targets for a broad range of diseases. The largest class of immune receptors are cell-surface proteins that bind secreted signaling proteins to elicit potent cellular responses, such as XXX. The breadth of possible signaling outcomes has armed the immune system with the ability to sense and respond to a nearly endless array of environmental cues. Conversely, dysregulation of ligand–-receptor interactions leads to a number of diseases, including XXX. Harnessing the immunomodulatory capabilities of these receptors constitutes a major step toward attaining full control over immune functions.

Attempts to administer immunomodulatory proteins have broadly resulted in dose-limiting toxicities due to two properties of immune cell signaling. First, immune receptors are seldom solely expressed on cells of a single function---distinct cell types express similar amounts and kinds of surface proteins. Second, the signal generated upon binding these receptors is heavily influenced by cellular context (immunomodulatory proteins are pleiotropic). As a result, ligands bind their cognate receptors on both target and off-target cells and induce distinct, counterproductive responses from each cell type. For example, interleukin-2 (IL-2), when administered systemically, binds IL-2 receptor on both regulatory T cells (T~reg~s) and natural killer (NK) cells, leading to expansion of both cell types. When the goal is elicit immunosuppression through activation of T~reg~s, the concurrent expansion of pro-inflammatory NK cells counteracts the desired immunosuppressive effects and leads to severe toxicities.

Protein engineering methods have improved the safety and efficacy of immunomodulatory proteins by driving binding toward target cells (i.e., eliciting cell-type selectivity). Amino-acid sequence mutations have achieved receptor-subunit--level affinity tuning, biasing binding based on differences in subunit expression levels. Multivalent ligand complexes have improved selectivity by exploiting increases in local concentration upon binding. Through these so-called avidity effects, multivalent molecules exhibit enhanced sensitivity to subtle differences in receptor density between populations of cells. Coordinated changes in affinity and valency have produced highly selective molecules. For example, tetravalent IL-2 with enhanced affinity for the T~reg~-associated $\alpha$ receptor subunit has selectively enhanced binding for T~reg~s over NK cells, thus reducing off-target toxicities. 

Protein engineering methods are limited by the coupled nature of receptor signaling and targeting. A drug's therapeutic effect is earned through signal-receptor binding, and valency and affinity engineering methods rely on the differential expression of the signal receptor on target cells. Moreover, receptors with desirable signaling properties are seldom uniquely expressed on target cells. As a result, the maximum achievable selectivity of these molecules is limited by the magnitude of signal receptor expression on off-target cells.

Multispecific ligand complexes decouple signaling from targeting to further improve cell-type selectivity. These molecules generally drive binding toward target cells through high-affinity "targeting" subunits (e.g., signal-incompetent cytokine muteins, antibodies, or de novo binders), whose cognate receptors are uniquely expressed on target cells. Once bound, multispecific molecules exert their effects locally either through avidity-driven binding of low-affinity "signaling" subunits (e.g., cytokine muteins, growth factors, or agonistic antibodies), or through local exposure/release of payloads (e.g., chemotherapeutics via antibody--drug conjugates, mRNA via targeted nanoparticles, or biotoxins via immunotoxins). In either case, target receptor binding is the key determinant of cell-type selectivity. Optimizing multispecific ligand design for target cell binding independently from signaling unlocks a vast number of potential surface proteins which, when targeted in some combination, might enable uniquely selective delivery to any given cell type.

The design process of multispecific proteins is bottlenecked by the combinatorial complexity of possible target combinations. Here, we aim to systematically explore the multi-receptor targeting space to identify key properties of multispecificity and guide drug design. We first leverage CITE-seq data with a series of high-throughput computational analyses to evaluate the selectivity of many possible surface target combinations. We find a mechanistic binding model to be the most robust and biologically interpretable metric of cell-type selectivity. Using this model, we find that at low valency, selectivity is optimized by maximizing the number of ligands for a single defining target receptor rather than employing multi-receptor targeting. We show that nearly every target exhibits synergy in selectivity when paired with some other receptor, but only high-valency, asymmetric ligand designs are able to exploit this synergy to achieve benefit beyond single-receptor targeting. Finally, we show that synergy arises as a result of dynamic differences in absolute expression between target receptors. In sum, these results point multispecific protein engineering efforts towards high-valency, asymmetric ligands that target receptors with variable expression in order to achieve optimal cell-type selectivity.
